On the night of Ramchandra Ray’s escape, Udayaditya is the active rescuer/escapee who commands Sitaram to open the door, draws his sword, overpowers the situation, and binds Sitaram at Sitaram’s own request so he will be spared punishment. On the night of Udayaditya’s own escape from prison, Sitaram becomes the active rescuer: he opens Udayaditya’s prison door, tells him the prison is on fire, almost carries him out, and instructs him, “Come, come with me,” while Udayaditya is passive, dependent, and asks what he should do and where he should go.

Pratapaditya’s initial plan was for two Pathan men to kill Basanta Ray when he sheltered at the inn in Simultali on his way to Jessore; this failed when the Pathan assigned to do it could not bring himself to carry it out. Finally, Muktiyar Khan came with soldiers and Pratapaditya’s signed death order, and Abdul killed Basanta Ray with a sword.
In the inner quarters—specifically the Mahishi’s room—disguised as a middle-aged woman, and in the room where the king and Ramai Bhand the jester were seated, in his jester role.
Surma takes the poison secretly prepared by Mangala at Rukmini’s instigation, and dies by her own hand.
Ramchandra Ray marries another woman, so when Vibha finally arrives, there is no place or home for her in her husband’s kingdom or royal palace, and all her hopes of happiness vanish.

Rukmini obtained Udayaditya’s signet ring from him; because it bore the Yubaraj’s name as a seal, it was used to stamp a forged petition accusing him of treason, which Bhagavat presented to Pratapaditya as evidence, leading to the order for Udayaditya’s imprisonment.

Ramchandra Ray’s midnight escape led to Sitaram and Bhagavat being dismissed; Udayaditya fixed monthly stipends for them, Pratapaditya forbade further help, Surma secretly arranged the stipends through a trusted maid, Mangala learned of it and word reached Pratapaditya, who then ordered Surma to go to her paternal home.

The song expresses loneliness and emptiness after loved ones have gone—those he once sang for no longer answer, what remains is emptiness/illusion, and singing no longer brings joy. Basanta Ray sings it in two contrasting contexts: in Raigarh, sitting on the palace veranda at sunset and humming to himself as he thinks of absent loved ones; and in Jessore, in the inner quarters, taking Vibha’s hand before the silent, dark, empty room after realizing “Those who were here before are here no more.”

After failing to stop the escape at the canal, Rukmini reported it to Pratapaditya, was sent with soldiers, and later pointed Udayaditya out to them in Raigarh; Udayaditya’s capture then led Muktiyar Khan to carry out Pratapaditya’s order sentencing Basanta Ray to death.

Pratapaditya receives Ramchandra Ray with cold indifference and superiority, barely acknowledging him and treating him as insignificant, while Ramchandra later addresses Pratapaditya’s status in his own court by repeatedly mocking, ridiculing, and belittling him as lowly and inferior.

The older widow from Raigarh is Rukmini, who left Raigarh, changed her name to Mangala, and lived on the outskirts of Jessore. The Rajmahishi, hearing that the widow Mangala knew tantra, mantra, and medicine, sent Matangini to secretly fetch medicine from her; Mangala spent the night preparing a poison with roots and mantras, and after five days of rituals prepared it so that Udayaditya would feel no pity when Surma died. With Pratapaditya’s consent, Surma was allowed to stay a few more days, and then Surma died after taking the poison—spreading the news that she had died by her own hand.

Udayaditya’s early lament culminates when, brought before Pratapaditya as a prisoner, he says he is not worthy of the kingdom and asks to be released from the throne; after Pratapaditya asks for proof of his heart, Udayaditya swears before Ma-Kali that he will never accept or touch the kingdom or royal scepter of Jessore and declares Samaraditya the heir, then leaves for Kashi.

Nayanchand diverted the letter to the Mahishi instead of delivering it to Pratapaditya; the Mahishi showed it to Basanta Ray, and they announced to Vibha and the household that Ramchandra had written requesting that Vibha be sent to Chandradwip.
The canal was blocked with large sal-wood logs, but Rammohan and his followers pulled the boat up and over the logs, allowing Ramchandra Ray to escape.

Basanta Ray leaves his sitar behind and says he will not play it anymore; later his “eternal companion” is no longer with him, and he says its strings have broken and it can no longer be tuned, while his singing no longer brings joy—reflecting his growing despair over being separated from Udayaditya and the loss of those he loved.

Earlier, Udayaditya had a reputation for involving himself in subjects’ affairs and for being willing to fight oppression and protect subjects without considering the consequences; after Surma’s death, his former courage was gone, he became fearful and hesitant, and he no longer dared to intervene—he called off his horse when hearing of the planned looting, ran inside upon seeing a subject beaten, and lacked the courage even to help Bhagavat and Sitaram secretly.
He opens Udayaditya’s prison during the fire, tells him the prison is on fire, and leads him out to freedom.

He ties sheets into a rope, fastens it to a roof pillar, carries Ramchandra on his back, climbs down, grips the rope with his teeth, and lowers Ramchandra into the boat; later, when Vibha faints, he lifts her and carries her out of the palace to a palanquin.

In Jessore, she is elaborately adorned by the Mahishi with thick gold bangles, huge diamond bracelets, a large nose ring, and a coiffure styled to the Mahishi’s taste, carrying the “burden” of ornaments and coiffure with shy joy. In Chandradwip, she refuses a palanquin and goes “like a common subject, like a beggar-woman,” dressed as a common woman; she enters the palace like any maidservant, with no welcome, and the king takes her for a beggar woman seeking alms.

In his bedchamber after Surma’s death, the window is where Surma used to sit and becomes a focus of his hope that she might return—he comes to it with “a flicker of hope” of seeing her there. In the prison cell, the small window shows a sliver of sky, bamboo grove, and Shiva temple; by looking at the sky and birds through it, Udayaditya thinks his “cage too will one day break” and he will be free, and he calls that small patch the place where he knows he is “naturally free,” while the soft bed is his prison.

The flirtatious moneylending relationship—Sitaram borrowing from Rukmini, joking about interest, and avoiding repayment—turns hostile when Sitaram curses and threatens Rukmini after Udayaditya’s imprisonment, saying he will set her house on fire, ruin her home, smear her face with lime and soot, and drive her from the city. Later, after the fire and Udayaditya’s escape, Sitaram goes to Rukmini’s cottage intending to take her money and finds her wet, disheveled, and seemingly returned from death; she threatens to lay him and the Yubaraj in the oven and smear herself with ashes from their pyres, then searches for a curved blade. Sitaram feigns affection, but Rukmini becomes enraged, and he slips out of the cottage; she strikes the floor where he had stood with the blade.

Sitaram first uses the guardhouse fire as a distraction: the guards run from Udayaditya’s door, and Sitaram enters the dark prison, tells Udayaditya the prison is on fire, and almost carries him out to escape. The strategy then becomes a cover-up: Sitaram’s men among the firefighters pour water where there is no fire, fail to bring water, break water pots, and create confusion so the fire will not go out; meanwhile his men set fire to Udayaditya’s empty prison cell—windows, doors, beams, rafters, doorframes, and wooden fences—and Sitaram throws in bones, a skull, and Udayaditya’s sword. He then shouts that the Yubaraj’s cell has caught fire and that the roof has collapsed with no response from him, leading everyone to believe Udayaditya died in the fire. Sitaram thinks he can spread the news that the Yubaraj died in the fire and remain untroubled for some time; he also takes back and destroys Udayaditya’s letters except those for the Mahishi and Vibha, and later the rumor of the Yubaraj’s death reaches Pratapaditya, with witnesses claiming they saw or heard Udayaditya and with the burnt remains of his sword produced from the cell.

Ramchandra Ray later treats Udayaditya’s rescue as nothing and joins his courtiers in laughing and joking about him; he believes Udayaditya saved him for the sake of his own sister, not out of concern for Ramchandra, and regards Udayaditya’s only “crime” as being Pratapaditya’s son.

A forged petition was written as if Udayaditya were lodging a complaint of treason against Pratapaditya with the Emperor of Delhi in order to get the kingdom for himself, and it was stamped with Udayaditya’s seal. Bhagavat then brought this petition to Pratapaditya, claiming that a servant of Udayaditya had been taking it toward Delhi and had fled. Thus the Emperor of Delhi became the apparent recipient of the son’s supposed treasonous appeal, and the petition was used as the mechanism against him.

In Chapter 8, Vibha secretly goes to Surma to have her hair done to her own liking, and the Mahishi notices the “flawed hairstyle,” perceives that Surma has purposely ruined Vibha’s hair out of jealousy, undoes it, and styles it again. In Chapter 18, after Surma is gone, when it is time to braid Vibha’s hair she sits quietly as if Surma will come at any moment to braid it, waits, but Surma does not come and her hair remains unbraided. In Chapter 23, Rammohan observes that Vibha’s hair is unkempt and says it seems there is no one there to care for her.
